## A finding is only as good as the measure

<!-- Lead with one concrete example. Best candidates:
     (a) rural Trump support gap that shrinks/grows depending on whether
         you use F_METRO vs. USR_SELFID in Pew ATP, or
     (b) rural attitudes toward immigration where RUCC and Cramer-style
         cultural-rural produce different stories.
     Two short paragraphs. Name the puzzle, don't resolve it yet. -->

The question is not whether rural Americans differ from urban Americans on
[X] — they do, on almost everything we measure. The question is *which* rural
Americans, and *how* we know. This post is about that second question, which
turns out to do more analytical work than most of us treat it as doing.

## Five ways to be rural

Most published work on rural political behavior reaches for one of five
operationalizations. Each measures something slightly different. None is
wrong. They are not interchangeable.

### Rural–Urban Continuum Codes (RUCC)

<!-- USDA, county-level, nine-point metro/non-metro scale. Most common in
     applied work. Available in the rurality package. -->

### Rural–Urban Commuting Areas (RUCA)

<!-- USDA, ZIP-level, commuting-flow-based. Finer grain. Useful when the
     county is too coarse — e.g. Los Angeles County contains both. -->

### Census/ATP metropolitan indicator (F_METRO)

<!-- Binary metro / non-metro. The default in most public-opinion datasets.
     Coarse but ubiquitous. -->

### Self-identified urban / suburban / rural (USR_SELFID)

<!-- Pew's USR variable. Captures cultural identification rather than
     geography. Diverges meaningfully from F_METRO — many suburban
     residents self-identify as rural. -->

### Cultural-rural (Cramer-style)

<!-- Not a variable on a file. A construct built from regional identity,
     resentment, and consumption patterns. Hardest to measure in
     existing data; most consequential for the dependent variables we
     actually care about. -->

## When the measures agree, and when they don't

<!-- Short empirical section. Use rurality + Pew ATP to show overlap
     statistics across measures. Probably one figure: 5x5 agreement
     matrix or a Sankey of how respondents flow across operationalizations.
     The "diagonal cases" are not the interesting ones; the off-diagonals
     are where the substantive findings get made or unmade. -->

A first-pass tabulation across Pew ATP Wave [W] illustrates the gap. Roughly
[X]% of respondents are classified the same way by all five measures. The
remaining [Y]% sit in a measurement no-man's-land where the choice of
instrument determines whether they appear in the "rural" cell of any given
crosstab.

## Why this is substantive, not housekeeping

<!-- The argument: the off-diagonal respondents are systematically different.
     Self-identified rural / geographically suburban respondents look more
     like Cramer's "rural consciousness" group than they do like their
     geographic neighbors. The choice of measure is therefore not neutral
     even when the headline N stays similar.

     One paragraph on the political-methodology framing: this is a latent-
     construct problem dressed up as a coding choice. -->
